Lemonade is a cold drink made by mixing lemon juice, water, and sugar together. That's the heart of it. The sourness of the lemon and the sweetness of the sugar balance each other out, making it a refreshing drink, especially in hot weather.
In its most common, classic form, lemonade is a pale yellow, slightly cloudy liquid. It looks a little like diluted yellow juice. It has a tangy, sweet smell and taste.

Here is something important to know: the word "lemonade" can mean slightly different things depending on where in the world you are.

1. Still lemonade (no bubbles)
This is the most traditional kind. It is simply fresh lemon juice squeezed from real lemons, mixed with water and sugar. It has no fizz. This is what most people in the United States picture when they hear the word "lemonade." Think of a child selling cups of it on a hot summer day — that's this kind.

2. Fizzy lemonade (with bubbles)
In countries like the United Kingdom and Australia, "lemonade" very commonly refers to a sweet, fizzy, carbonated soft drink with a lemon flavour — something like a clear, lemon-flavoured soda. It's bubbly, like a cola or sparkling water. This version often doesn't contain fresh lemon juice at all — it's a manufactured soft drink. In these countries, if you want the non-fizzy, freshly-squeezed kind, you'd often ask for "cloudy lemonade" or "homemade lemonade" to be clear.

So, the same word, but two very different drinks depending on the country. If you ever order lemonade while travelling, keep this in mind!

Beyond the two main types, you'll often see these popular variations:

  • Pink lemonade — Still lemonade that has been tinted pink (and slightly flavoured) by adding fruits like strawberries, raspberries, or cherries. It tastes similar to regular lemonade but is slightly fruitier.
  • Sparkling lemonade — This is the still (American-style) lemonade but made fizzy by using carbonated water instead of plain water. Think of it as a middle ground between the two main types.
  • Mint lemonade — A popular variation, especially in the Middle East, where fresh mint leaves are blended in. It is very refreshing.
How the Word Behaves in a Sentence

Lemonade is usually an uncountable noun, meaning you don't normally say "a lemonade" or "two lemonades" when talking about the drink itself. Instead, you say:

  • "Can I have some lemonade?"
  • "She drank a glass of lemonade."
  • "He made a pitcher of lemonade."
  • "There's no lemonade left."

However, in informal settings — like at a café or restaurant — people do sometimes use it as a countable noun when ordering servings:

  • "Two lemonades, please." (meaning two glasses/cups of lemonade)
  • "They serve several different lemonades here." (meaning several varieties)

Both are natural and correct in everyday speech.
A Famous Phrase Connected to This Word

You will almost certainly encounter this expression in English at some point:

"When life gives you lemons, make lemonade."

This is one of the most well-known idioms in the English language. Here's what it means:

Lemons on their own are very sour and not pleasant to eat raw — they represent something bad, difficult, or disappointing that happens in life. But lemonade, made from those lemons, is delicious and enjoyable — it represents turning a negative situation into something positive.

So the phrase means: when something bad happens to you, try to find a way to make the best of it. It's an expression of optimism and resilience. You'll hear it used as advice or encouragement.
